title: Pain at the Thumb Side of the Wrist: De Quervain's Tendon Pain Explained
metaDescription: Pain at the thumb side of the wrist, worse with gripping or phone use, may be De Quervain's tenosynovitis. Causes, treatment steps and warning signs explained.
intro: Pain on the thumb side of the wrist that is worse when you grip, pinch or turn the wrist is often De Quervain's tenosynovitis. It means the covering (sheath) around two thumb tendons is irritated and thickened. Symptoms normally settle in 6 to 12 weeks with simple measures. A doctor can usually diagnose it by examining your wrist, without a scan.

sections.heading: What does De Quervain's tendon pain feel like?
sections.body: You feel pain and tenderness at the base of the thumb and on the thumb side of the wrist. It is worse with gripping, pinching, making a fist or turning the wrist. There may be swelling there, and sometimes catching when you move the thumb. The pain can travel up the forearm.

sections.heading: Who gets it, and why?
sections.body: The exact cause is not fully understood, but repeated wrist and thumb movements such as typing, texting and lifting can make it worse. It is most common in people in their 40s and 50s and affects more women than men. It is also linked to pregnancy and the weeks after having a baby, and rheumatoid arthritis may make it more likely.

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed?
sections.body: Your doctor listens to your history and examines the wrist. In Finkelstein's test, you tuck your thumb into your palm, close your fingers over it and bend the wrist towards the little finger. Pain during this movement suggests De Quervain's. A scan is not normally needed, but may be done if the diagnosis is unclear.

sections.heading: What is our usual approach to treatment?
sections.body: We begin with the gentlest steps and tailor them to you.
bullets: Medicines first: anti-inflammatory tablets such as ibuprofen, or gels, can ease pain and swelling. Not everyone can take them, so ask a pharmacist or doctor what suits you.
Rest and ice: avoid painful activities where you can. A cool pack wrapped in a cloth for 15 to 20 minutes, three times a day, may help.
Splint: a removable splint keeps the wrist straight and the thumb still, especially at night or during aggravating tasks.
Exercises: once pain eases, a therapist can show you ways to reduce strain and gentle strengthening.
Physiotherapy machines such as ultrasound or short-wave: if used, these are for pain relief only, and the evidence for them is modest.

sections.heading: Is a steroid injection worth considering?
sections.body: If symptoms do not settle in the expected time, a steroid injection into the painful area can reduce swelling and relieve pain. Many people improve after one. It is not suitable for everyone, as some health conditions and medicines make it unsafe, and people with diabetes may respond less well. How long relief lasts varies, so we offer it only to selected people, for pain relief, alongside changes to the activities that strain the thumb.

sections.heading: Will I need surgery?
sections.body: Most people do not. Surgery is considered if symptoms are severe or have not improved after about 6 weeks of non-surgical treatment. The surgeon opens the sheath to give the tendons more room, taking care to protect nearby nerves. It is usually a same-day procedure, and complications are rare. People with diabetes have a higher risk of infection or slow wound healing. We explain your options, and the decision is yours.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor quickly?
sections.body: Get assessed promptly if the swollen area becomes red or significantly hot, or if you feel generally unwell, as this can be a sign of infection. Come in too if the pain follows an injury, if you cannot move the thumb, or if symptoms have not settled after 6 to 12 weeks.

faqs.q: How long does De Quervain's tendon pain last?
faqs.a: Symptoms normally settle in 6 to 12 weeks. If yours have not, ask for a review.

faqs.q: Do I need an X-ray or scan?
faqs.a: Usually not. Diagnosis is based on your history and specific tests such as Finkelstein's test.

faqs.q: Why do new mothers get thumb-side wrist pain?
faqs.a: It is linked to pregnancy and the period after birth, with symptoms often appearing within 4 to 6 weeks of having a baby. Lifting and holding a baby also strain the thumb.
A removable splint keeps the wrist straight and the thumb still, and is often most helpful at night.

faqs.q: Can I keep using my phone and computer?
faqs.a: Usually yes, in moderation. Take breaks and avoid movements that bring on the pain until it settles.

faqs.q: Is it the same as carpal tunnel syndrome?
faqs.a: No. Carpal tunnel mainly causes numbness and tingling in the fingers, while De Quervain's causes pain at the thumb side of the wrist.
